questions.question: Write the differences between sulphitation and carbonation.
questions.solution_html:
• Ans
  • Sulphitation
  • Involves adding sulphur dioxide (SO₂) to cane juice.
  • Prevents browning and acts as a preservative.
  • Carbonation
  • Involves addition of lime (Ca(OH)₂) and CO₂ to remove impurities.
  • Used for clarification of juice.
  • Direct Method In this method, chocolate is melted directly in a microwave
  • oven. • Heat the chocolate at 50% power and check every 20 seconds. • When
  • most of it melts and a few small lumps remain, take it out. • Stir well — the
  • remaining lumps will melt with the heat. • This method is quick and easy, but if
  • heated too long, the chocolate can overheat and burn.
  • Melt chocolate and butter together.
  • Wheat Flour
  • Major ingredient in bread making.
  • Obtained through the milling process, where the bran and germ parts of the wheat grain are
  • removed.
  • Main components of flour
  • o Moisture – 14%
  • o Starch – 70%
  • o Protein – 11%
  • o Ash – 1.5%
  • o Sugar – 1%
  • o Fat – 1%
  • Characteristics of Good Quality Flour
  • Appearance
  • Flour should be creamy white and smooth.
  • It should not contain bran pieces (brown flakes from wheat’s outer layer).
  • Strength
  • Flour should be strong so the dough keeps its shape.
  • This strength comes from good gluten, which helps the bread rise well.
  • Water Absorption
  • Good flour absorbs more water and forms a soft, stretchy dough.
  • It needs less mixing to form properly.
  • This makes the bread light and fluffy after baking.
  • Helps form gluten – Water mixes with flour proteins (gliadin and glutenin) to make
  • elastic gluten, which gives the dough structure.
  • Plain Lozenges
  • Made by cutting pieces from a sheet of dough.
  • These pieces are then dried in air.
  • No special shaping is needed.
  • Mixing
  • Ingredients like sugar, gum arabic/gelatine, stearine, and flavouring are mixed well.
  • Proper mixing gives the lozenges good shape and brittleness.
  • Chocolate contains cocoa butter, a type of fat.
  • Temperature changes (warm → cool → warm)
  • Temper chocolate properly – so the fat sets correctly.
  • Mixing of Ingredients
  • Sugar, glucose, water, gelatin, fat, and other ingredients are mixed together to form a
  • smooth, uniform paste.
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025
questions.final_answer: smooth, uniform paste.

questions.question: What are unshortened cakes?
questions.solution_html:
• Ans
  • Also called foam cakes.
  • Do not contain fat.
  • Egg whites are beaten to trap air.
  • Leavened by air and steam during baking.
  • Texture is light, fluffy, and spongy.
  • Very little or no oil used.
  • Examples: angel food cake, sponge cake.
  • What is gur?
  • Ans : Gur, also called jaggery, is a natural sweetener made from sugarcane juice. It is
  • brown or golden in color and is used in many Indian sweets. Gur is healthier than white
  • sugar and is full of natural minerals. Sources of Gur: Mainly from sugarcane Also made
  • from palmyra, date palm, and coconut sap . Color - Golden yellow to brown
  • Seeding Method • This is the most common professional method. • Melt 2/3
  • of the chocolate and then add 1/3 chopped solid chocolate (called seeds). • Stir
  • until the added pieces melt completely. • The solid pieces help cool and stabilize
  • the melted chocolate, giving it a smooth, shiny finish.
  • Cook the syrup to soft ball stage (112°C).
  • Softens starch – Makes the starch in flour soft and easy to digest after baking.
  • Yeast
  • The main function of yeast is to make the dough light and spongy and to give bread its
  • pleasant aroma and flavour.
  • The yeast used in bread making is Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
  • Yeast uses the fermentable sugars present in the dough during the fermentation process.
  • Through enzyme action, yeast produces carbon dioxide gas and alcohol.
  • The carbon dioxide gas gets trapped in the gluten network, causing the dough to rise and
  • become soft and airy.
  • During fermentation, small amounts of alcohol and acids are also produced.
  • o These soften (mellow) the gluten, making the dough easy to stretch.
  • o The acids contribute to the characteristic flavour of the bread.
  • Yeast is available in two main forms
  • o Compressed yeast (fresh yeast)
  • o Dried yeast (active dry yeast or instant yeast)
  • Drying
  • The drying temperature should not exceed 105°F.
  • Lozenges should not be kept longer than necessary in the drying stage.

  • Key Features of Fat Bloom
  • White/gray patches on chocolate
  • Chocolate becomes soft, loses shine
  • Texture becomes grainy and dull
  • Taste remains safe, but quality reduces
  • Main Causes of Fat Bloom
  • Using different/low-quality fats
  • Avoid keeping in fridge – condensation causes bloom.
  • Mixing & Homogenization
  • The paste is stirred and pressed under pressure to make it smooth and consistent.

questions.question: Write a note on fermentation during bread making ?
questions.solution_html:
• Ans
  • Fermentation is the process where yeast acts on sugars in the dough.
  • It is an anaerobic process that takes place without oxygen.
  • It starts immediately after mixing and continues during inter proofing and
  • final proofing.
  • The main purpose of fermentation is to produce carbon dioxide gas which
  • makes the dough rise.
  • It also helps to develop flavour and aroma in the bread.
  • Fermentation improves the dough texture and makes it soft.
  • Ideal temperature for fermentation is between 24°C and 30°C.
  • Ideal humidity is about 70% to 75%.
  • These conditions are best for yeast activity and proper fermentation.
  • Usually 2% baker’s yeast (based on flour weight) is used.
  • Too little yeast causes slow fermentation.
  • Too much yeast gives sour Flavors and poor texture.
  • During fermentation, glucose (sugar) is converted by yeast into carbon
  • dioxide and alcohol.
  • Carbon dioxide makes the dough rise, and alcohol evaporates during baking.
  • Well-fermented dough becomes light, soft, and airy.
  • Bread made from properly fermented dough has good volume, taste, and
  • texture.
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025
questions.final_answer: texture.

questions.question: What is sugarcane ? Write down its nutritive value.
questions.solution_html:
• Sugarcane
  • Sugarcane is the chief source of sugar. It contains 12–15% sugar (mainly sucrose). In India
  • about 80–90% of sugarcane is used for the manufacture of sugar, gur, khandsari, and
  • other products.
  • It is also used for making beverages, chewing cane, and various sugar products.
  • Nutrient Amount
  • Energy 40–60 kcal
  • Carbohydrates 10–15 g
  • Sugars (Sucrose, Glucose, Fructose) 9–13 g
  • Protein 0.1 g
  • Fat 0 g
  • Nutrient Amount
  • Fiber 0 g
  • Calcium 10–15 mg
  • Potassium 150–200 mg
  • Iron 0.3 mg
  • Magnesium 10–12 mg
  • Sugarcane contains sucrose, glucose, and fructose.
  • Used for white sugar, gur (jaggery), khandsari, and molasses.
  • 5–10% of sugarcane is used for chewing.
  • It provides quick energy due to high sugar content.
  • Good source of potassium, calcium, and iron.

questions.question: How cocoa powder is produced ?
questions.solution_html:
• Steps in Cocoa Powder Production
  • Harvesting
  • Ripe cocoa pods are cut from the trees using knives or machetes.
  • Pod Opening
  • The pods are split open and the beans with pulp are removed.
  • Fermentation
  • Beans are fermented for 5–7 days to develop flavour, reduce bitterness, and remove pulp.
  • Drying
  • Fermented beans are dried in the sun or dryers until moisture reaches 6–7%.
  • Breaking and Winnowing
  • Dried beans are cracked (breaking) and shells are removed to get cocoa nibs.
  • Alkalisation (Dutching)
  • Nibs are treated with alkali (e.g., potassium carbonate) to improve colour, flavour, and
  • dispersibility.
  • Roasting
  • Alkalised nibs are roasted at 120–150°C to enhance flavour and reduce moisture.
  • Nib Grinding
  • Roasted nibs are ground into a thick paste called cocoa liquor (or cocoa mass).
  • Liquor Treatment (Pressing)
  • Cocoa liquor is pressed to separate cocoa butter.
  • The solid cake left behind is used for cocoa powder.
  • Pulverisation
  • The cocoa cake is crushed and ground into fine cocoa powder.
  • Packing
  • The cocoa powder is sieved and packed in airtight, moisture-proof containers or bags
  • to prevent spoilage.
  • Storage
  • Packed powder is stored in cool, dry conditions, away from light and strong odours to
  • maintain quality.
  • Transport
  • Finished cocoa powder is transported in sealed containers or cartons to protect it from
  • moisture, heat, and contamination.
